questions.text: To start, how would you describe the kind of physical design work you do?
And historically if we look at the design practice you had in this field from the past?
What do you actually produce - concepts, physical products, production-ready data, digital content?
Where does your involvement start and where does it stop?
How long have you been in the practice?
Has the kind of work shifted over that time?
Is there design work you do for yourself, outside paid work?
What scale did you work at - one-offs, small series, mass production? Who paid?
How much of what you designed actually reached production - and would you know?
Can you walk us through your last complex project, from the moment it started for you to the moment it went to production or was deemed finished?
Where did most of your effort actually go?
Which of those takes longest?
Was any of it work you would not call design?
What was information before you started - platform, tooling, brand language?
Was there a brief at all - who formulated it, and in what form?
How much effort goes into positioning the work internally - what you show, to whom, when?
Please describe your screen at a normal working moment. What is open, what is lying around the desk?
What kind of modeling would you do? software.
Was this selected for you or is it your personal choice?
How does inheriting a project works?
How do you build a project so it survives change later?
What does a fragile model look like when you open one?
Do you build differently when you know it is a one-off?
Where do versions live - PDM, folders, filenames?
Anything in your stack you are not officially licensed for?
How does a material get chosen on a project?
At what point is material decided, by whom, and against what else is that budget weighed?
What do you go on - datasheet, supplier, past project, feel?
What do you know about a material that is not on its datasheet?
Where did you learn that - who told you, or what went wrong?
Has that knowledge ever turned out to be wrong?
Would you pass it on, or does it have to be earned?
Where does that knowledge live - a database, a sample shelf, a person?
How do cost, sustainability, or regulation enter the choice?
A material you wanted to use and could not
Does the material budget compete with components elsewhere in the product?
Has a material decision been reversed months later? What did that cost you?
Does the work become physical before production, or does it stay as data?
Walk us through the last thing that was prototyped for you. Why did you print it? ↳ concrete-instance probe
What are you checking - form, fit, function, or showing someone?
What is the prototyping process/material you found most helpfull?
What decides it - the object itself, or what the audience expects to see?
What does the physical part tell you that the screen does not?
Does the number of rounds change with the kind of project - a refresh vs. something new?
Where do the rejected prototypes end up?
Is there an expected level of finish for showing work, and who set that expectation?
What happens when a design does not get through review - and how far does your involvement reach?
When do people intervien?
Is the objection about the design, or about the brief being wrong?
Manufacturability feedback: when does it arrive, and is that too late?
How do you consolidate incompatible feedback?
When is a direction declared dead, and how late can that still happen?
When a project is killed late, what happens to the work already done?
Who else has their hands on a project alongside you?
Engineering, tooling, suppliers, clients - who is unavoidable and who is chosen?
Several people on one model: simultaneous or sequential?
How does a handoff actually happen?
Where does the conversation about a project happen?
Where is the friction sharpest?
When you want useful feedback, who do you actually go to - and is that who you are supposed to ask?
Whose arguments count as decisive, and whose have to be wrapped in something else?
How would you describe someone who is really good at this work?
How did you learn this - training, or on the work?
What does an experienced designer know that a new one does not?
Templates, saved settings, own libraries - anything you built for yourself?
What do you know that is not written down anywhere?
How long until someone new is fully productive?
Something you do that you know is not the proper method
What does a mistake look like in your work?
A mistake caught in CAD vs. in a prototype vs. in tooling: what changes?
How are mistakes caught, and what happens then?
Caught by you, or by someone else?
Does it get recorded anywhere, or just fixed?
Does the same kind of mistake come back?
Have you ever lost a model or a revision? What happened?
Do you trust simulation, or do you need the physical part?
Which part of the process do you trust the least?
Tolerances: where do they come from and who owns them?
Has anything in your work been automated over the years? How did that go?
AI or generative tools in use today, officially or on the side
Generative design or topology optimisation - used, ignored, or distrusted?
Do you proof check what it produces, and how?
Automation imposed vs. adopted: attitudes
If one part of the work could be handed off tomorrow, which one?
